title: API Design Deep Practices
summary: Idempotent writes, filtering and sorting without URL sprawl, and a consistent error format — the practices that separate a working API from a production-ready one.

slides.markdown:
A REST API that only gets the nouns-and-verbs shape right still breaks in production: a client's dropped connection retries a `POST` and double-charges a card, or a mobile app has to fetch and discard 90% of a payload just to render a list row.

This topic covers the practices that fix that: making writes safe to retry, letting clients shape the response instead of over- or under-fetching, and returning errors in one predictable shape. These are the details an interviewer digs into once the basic REST shape is already assumed.

slides.sectionTitle: Idempotency in APIs: safe retries for POST
slides.markdown:
An operation is **idempotent** if calling it once has the same effect as calling it many times. `GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are idempotent by HTTP convention — fetching, replacing, or removing the same resource repeatedly leaves the system in the same end state. `POST` is not: by default, calling `POST /charges` twice creates two charges.

This matters because networks fail silently in the worst way — a client sends a request, the server processes it, but the response is lost before the client sees it. The client can't tell "my request never arrived" from "it arrived and succeeded, but I didn't hear back," so its only safe move is to retry — and a non-idempotent endpoint turns that safe move into a duplicate charge.

The fix isn't to ban retries; it's to make the operation safe to repeat, which the next slide covers.

An **idempotency key** is a client-generated unique token (usually a UUID) sent as a header on a `POST`, e.g. `Idempotency-Key: 9c1f...`. The server stores the key alongside the result of the first request it processes. If the same key arrives again — because the client retried after a timeout — the server returns the **stored result** instead of re-running the operation.

The client generates the key once per logical operation (not per HTTP attempt) and reuses it on every retry of that same attempt. The server typically keeps the key-to-result mapping for a bounded window — long enough to cover realistic retry storms (minutes to a day), not forever.

This is the standard pattern payment APIs (Stripe, for example) use to make `POST /charges` safe to retry without double-charging.

slides.sectionTitle: Filtering, sorting, and partial responses without blowing up the URL
slides.markdown:
As a resource collection grows, clients need to filter (`status=active`), sort (`sort=-created_at`), and shrink the response to only the fields they use (`fields=id,name,total`). All three belong in **query parameters**, not the path — `/orders?status=active&sort=-created_at&fields=id,total` keeps the path stable (`/orders`) while the query string carries every variation.

Partial responses (field selection) matter more than they look: a mobile list view that only needs `id`, `name`, and `total` shouldn't have to download every field of every order, especially over a slow connection. Letting the client name the fields it wants avoids both over-fetching (wasted bytes) and the alternative of maintaining a separate lightweight endpoint per view.

The discipline: the path names the resource, the query string names the view of it.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a request with filter/sort/field-selection params
slides.markdown:
![A single request URL broken into resource, filter, sort, and field-selection segments](assets/query-param-anatomy.svg)

One request, three independent concerns layered into the query string: which rows come back (filter), what order they arrive in (sort), and which fields each row includes (field selection). None of them change what resource is being addressed — that's still `/orders`.

Keeping them additive and independent (any combination is valid) is what lets the same endpoint serve a dashboard, a mobile list, and an export job without three separate routes.

slides.sectionTitle: Consistent error response format across an API
slides.markdown:
Every endpoint in an API should return errors in the **same shape** — a machine-readable `code`, a human-readable `message`, and optionally per-field `details` — regardless of which team or service handled the request. Without this, every client integration ends up writing custom parsing per endpoint, because one team's 404 body looks nothing like another's.

A shared shape typically looks like:

```
{ "error": { "code": "VALIDATION_FAILED", "message": "Request could not be processed", "details": [ { "field": "email", "issue": "invalid format" } ] } }
```

The `code` is what client code branches on (stable, machine-checkable); the `message` is what a developer reads in logs; `details` gives enough to point a user at the exact field to fix.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: rich query params vs a dedicated query/search endpoint
slides.markdown:
| | Rich query params on the collection | Dedicated query/search endpoint |
|---|---|---|
| URL | `GET /orders?status=active&min_total=100` | `POST /orders/search` with a JSON query body |
| Complexity ceiling | Fine for a handful of simple filters | Handles nested boolean logic, full-text search, complex sorts |
| Cacheability | `GET` + URL is cacheable by default | `POST` body isn't cached by standard HTTP caching |
| Discoverability | Self-describing in the URL | Needs its own documented query language |

**How to decide:** start with query params — they're simpler and cacheable. Reach for a dedicated search endpoint only once filters genuinely need boolean combinations, full-text ranking, or a query shape too complex to encode legibly in a query string.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a non-idempotent POST that double-charges on a client retry
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Our client has retry logic for network errors, so the API is resilient."

**Why it's wrong:** if `POST /charges` has no idempotency key, a retry after a timed-out-but-actually-successful request creates a second charge. The client did the right thing (retrying on an ambiguous failure); the API made that safe behavior dangerous by treating every `POST` as brand new.

**Correct model:** any `POST` that a client might reasonably retry — payments, order creation, anything with a real-world side effect — needs an idempotency key so a retry returns the original result instead of repeating the effect. Resilience on the client only helps if the server-side operation is actually safe to repeat.

slides.sectionTitle: API versioning: URI, header, and additive-only strategies
slides.subTitle: Versioning
slides.markdown:
Every API eventually needs a breaking change, and deciding how clients discover which version they're talking to is a decision the schema and the error format above both assume is already solved.

Three common approaches: **URI versioning** (`/v1/orders`, `/v2/orders`) is the most visible and cache-friendly, but forces you to maintain parallel URL trees. **Header versioning** (`Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=2`) keeps URLs stable but is easy for API consumers to get wrong or forget. **No explicit version, additive-only changes** avoids the whole problem by treating every change as backward-compatible (new optional fields only, never removing or repurposing a field) — Stripe famously runs this way, pinning each account to a dated version instead of a number.

The takeaway: pick the versioning scheme before your first breaking change is unavoidable — retrofitting it onto a live API with existing clients is far more painful than deciding it up front.
